sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the UNIVERSE-ENGINE-ASTER sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. The children enter the installation with which Aster launched the autonomous memorial universes. The memorial bore the name of Egan; cosmological engineering precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. A machine became interesting when its purpose entered history. A self-replicator did not remain an engineering diagram after its first century; it became ecology, economy, a possible species, and sometimes an adversary. Marae kept her local body vulnerable. Pain, fatigue, and the impossibility of doing ten things at once were epistemic instruments for her, not biological scenery. The children were met by Noor, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster 265 admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. The problem closed quickly around them: They discover that many worlds are not educational simulations but realities with irreversible consequences, created and observed in order to treat the Hunger. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ua — Artificial Universe: intelligences manufacture baby universes; Go — World Grammar: elements combine as a language of design. Course references included cosmological engineering SF; original concept. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became 266 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Orin says that “we stopped long ago” is a consolation for the creator, not for the victims of old experiments. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the EXTERNALIZATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — turns an internal property into an object, companion, infrastructure, or institution — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy 267 of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 268 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 269 PART 10​ THE OTHER THAT DOES NOT WANT TO BE UNDERSTOOD A period in the curriculum of the five children 270 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
